---
title: "Fisher's exact test"
execute:
  enabled: true
  echo: true
  warning: false
  message: false
---

Fisher's exact test evaluates association in a two-by-two table by conditioning on
both observed margins. Under a null odds ratio of one, the remaining free cell has
a hypergeometric distribution. This conditional reference distribution is
distinct from the multivariate-hypergeometric randomness induced by drawing 120
lexemes without replacement from the 588-row table: the sampling design does not
itself fix the two sample margins.

Here [conditioning](../foundations/conditional-probability.qmd) means calculating
probabilities after treating the observed row and column totals as given, while
the null [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd#why-the-characterizations-are-equivalent)
model says the joint cell probabilities factorize into their marginals.

The present analysis therefore contains two different operations: sampling 120
lexeme rows from the 588-row table and, after observing them, conditioning on the
sample table's margins. The derivation below keeps their two reference
distributions separate.

## A Turkish morphology sample

We use the [exact analyzed version of the Turkish UniMorph
release](https://github.com/unimorph/tur/tree/6c179ace7d2f3d7f3484020e5304c1544d07bb6b)
under CC BY-SA 3.0. Pimentel et al.
([2021](https://aclanthology.org/2021.sigmorphon-1.25/)) use the resource for
morphological reinflection: predicting an inflected form from a lemma and feature
bundle. The release describes its Turkish verb paradigms as semi-automatically
generated and partially checked by a native speaker; unverified noun and adjective
material is excluded from the analyzed verb population.

Each row represents one lexeme--paradigm cell: one of 588 distinct verb
lemmas paired with `V;IND;PST;3;SG;POS;DECL`. Corpus token frequencies do not
enter this table. The table retains the whole UniMorph form and derives the
last stem-vowel class and final two orthographic characters. We use those
analyst-derived characters as orthographic measurements; the source does not
mark them as morpheme boundaries. The release's [version-specific
README](https://github.com/unimorph/tur/blob/6c179ace7d2f3d7f3484020e5304c1544d07bb6b/README.md)
documents the source data and verification status.

### Two parts of the Turkish past-tense form {#turkish-past-allomorphy-map}

The derived two-character ending combines two phonological alternations. Its vowel
harmonizes with the last vowel of the stem: stems in *a/ı*, *e/i*, *o/u*, and
*ö/ü* take *ı*, *i*, *u*, and *ü*, respectively. Its initial consonant is *t*
after one of the voiceless stem-final consonants *ç, f, h, k, p, s, ş,* and *t*;
otherwise it is *d*. Thus last-vowel class predicts the suffix vowel, while
stem-final voicing predicts the *d*/*t* choice.

The Fisher analysis uses the 120-lemma simple random sample drawn without
replacement with seed 414. It deliberately crosses last stem-vowel backness with
the *d*/*t* initial. Both variables describe the same lexeme row, which makes a
valid independence table, but last-vowel backness is not the phonological
conditioner of the consonant alternation. The following comparison checks the canonical
conditioner before we construct the contingency table.

```{r}
#| label: load-unimorph-fisher
library(ggplot2)

population <- read.csv(
  "data/unimorph-turkish/verb-past-population.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
sample_120 <- read.csv(
  "data/unimorph-turkish/verb-past-sample-120.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
sample_120$front_vowel <- grepl("^front", sample_120$vowel_class)

canonical_tab <- table(
  stem_final_voiceless = sample_120$stem_final_voiceless,
  t_initial = sample_120$t_initial
)
stopifnot(all(sample_120$stem_final_voiceless == sample_120$t_initial))
canonical_tab

tab <- table(
  front_vowel = sample_120$front_vowel,
  t_initial = sample_120$t_initial
)
stopifnot(nrow(population) == 588L, nrow(sample_120) == 120L)
tab
```

The first table is diagonal because every sampled *t*-initial form follows a
stem-final consonant classified as voiceless by the preparation rule, and every
sampled *d*-initial form follows another stem-final segment. The second table asks
a different, intentionally noncanonical question: whether last-vowel backness and
the consonant initial are associated in these 120 sampled lexeme rows.

## The conditional probability

With row and column margins fixed, one cell determines the remaining cells. If $A$ is the front-vowel/*t*-initial count, then under the conditional independence model

$$
\mathbb{P}(A=a)
=\frac{{K\choose a}{N-K\choose n-a}}{{N\choose n}},
$$

where $K$ is the *t*-initial column total, $N-K$ is the *d*-initial total, and $n$ is the front-vowel row total.

To see the counting argument, imagine the $N$ sampled lexeme rows as $K$ *t*-initial rows and $N-K$ *d*-initial rows. A table with $A=a$ chooses $a$ of the $K$ *t*-initial rows and $n-a$ of the $N-K$ *d*-initial rows for the fixed front-vowel margin. There are ${K\choose a}{N-K\choose n-a}$ such choices out of ${N\choose n}$ possible size-$n$ front-vowel sets. This is the [hypergeometric probability](../random-variables-and-distributions/hypergeometric-distribution.qmd#mass-mean-and-variance).

The feasible values run from $\max(0,n-(N-K))$ through $\min(n,K)$. For each feasible $a$, the other three cells are forced by the margins. Thus Fisher's reference distribution enumerates complete tables even though it needs only one free cell.

```{r}
#| label: fit-unimorph-fisher
observed_a <- tab["TRUE", "1"]
t_total <- sum(tab[, "1"])
d_total <- sum(tab[, "0"])
front_total <- sum(tab["TRUE", ])
observed_probability <- dhyper(observed_a, t_total, d_total, front_total)
result <- fisher.test(tab, alternative = "two.sided")

summary <- data.frame(
  sample_size = nrow(sample_120),
  population_size = nrow(population),
  sampling_fraction = nrow(sample_120) / nrow(population),
  observed_table_probability = observed_probability,
  conditional_odds_ratio = unname(result$estimate),
  confidence_lower = result$conf.int[1],
  confidence_upper = result$conf.int[2],
  two_sided_p_value = result$p.value
)
summary
```

The observed table has conditional probability `r sprintf("%.5f", observed_probability)`. R's two-sided p value sums all fixed-margin tables whose null probability is no greater than the observed table's probability; it is `r sprintf("%.4f", result$p.value)`.

This last convention matters. A two-sided ordering is not unique for a discrete asymmetric reference distribution; `fisher.test()` uses the probability ordering just described, rather than merely doubling one tail.

```{r}
#| label: plot-unimorph-fisher
#| fig-cap: "Observed lexeme counts in the fixed UniMorph sample."
cells <- as.data.frame(tab, responseName = "lexemes")
cells$stem_vowel <- ifelse(cells$front_vowel == "TRUE", "Front", "Back")
cells$past_initial <- ifelse(cells$t_initial == "1", "t", "d")

ggplot(cells, aes(past_initial, stem_vowel, fill = lexemes)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = lexemes), size = 4) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "grey90", high = "grey45", guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Past sequence initial", y = "Last stem-vowel class") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The calculation conditions on both table margins after the `r nrow(sample_120)` rows have been
sampled. It supplies an exact conditional reference distribution under the null
model. The without-replacement design still matters for claims about repeated
samples from the 588-row table: its sampling fraction is
`r sprintf("%.3f", summary$sampling_fraction)`, and an independent Bernoulli model
would not reproduce that design. But this finite sampling fraction is not what
produces Fisher's fixed-margin distribution. The result concerns association
among UniMorph lexeme--paradigm rows; no corpus-token frequencies enter the table.

## Recap and forward link

1. Fixed margins leave one free cell in a two-by-two table.
2. Combinatorial counting yields a hypergeometric reference probability for that cell.
3. R's two-sided p value sums tables no more probable than the observed one; it is not the observed-table probability alone.
4. Exact conditioning does not turn lexeme types into usage tokens.

The [chi-squared page](chi-squared-test.qmd#expected-counts-under-independence) uses the complete 588-lemma resource for the corresponding large-sample calculation.

## Check your understanding

1. Which margins remain fixed in the Fisher reference distribution?
2. Why is the observed-table probability not the two-sided p value?
3. What does one UniMorph row represent?
4. Why can this table not estimate suffix frequency in running Turkish text?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The front/back row totals, the *t*/*d* column totals, and thus the grand total remain fixed. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The two-sided p value sums the probabilities of all fixed-margin tables no more probable under the null than the observed table. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. One row is one distinct verb lemma paired with the `V;IND;PST;3;SG;POS;DECL` paradigm cell. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. UniMorph rows are lexeme--paradigm types without corpus token frequencies, so the table cannot estimate how often suffixes occur in running text. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
